text: are novel thera- peutic approaches for PTLD.9 Cardiac allograft vasculop- athy (also termed coronary artery vasculopathy, or chronic rejection) is a major cause of death and prevention of its progression is a major therapeutic goal.2,3,9,32,33 It is thought to be mainly an immunological response, but can be accelerated by the classical risk factors of dyslipidae- mia, obesity, glucose intolerance, and smoking, as well as by postoperative CMV infection, and immunosuppression itself.3,6,8,34 Long-term use of calcineurin inhibitors is as- sociated with renal dysfunction and also contributes to hy- pertension and hyperlipidaemia, all of which may exacer- bate cardiac allograft vasculopathy.33 Calcium-channel blockers have been used to decrease the incidence of cor- onary artery disease, but it has remained a difficult compli- cation to treat.34 HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors such as pravastatin and simvastatin are recommended35,36 for the treatment of hyperlipidaemia; pravastatin or atorvastatin have been used in paediatric heart transplant patients.2 There is evidence that statin therapy substantially im- proves survival.37 Fibric acid derivatives may be consid- ered in those patients with hypertriglyceridaemia not con- trolled by diet alone.36 Supplementation with antoxidant vitamins such as C or E may reduce the progression of ar- teriosclerosis after transplantation,38 and a small study39 found that omega-3 fatty acids improved blood pressure control in hypertensive transplant recipients. There is some suggestion that sirolimus26,40 and everolimus41 may be of benefit in preventing cardiac allograft vasculopathy in adults; data are lacking in paediatric patients.2,9 Retrans- plantation for graft failure due to cardiac allograft vascu- lopathy may be necessary.33 Improved surgical techniques and the use of ciclosporin have also made possible successful combined heart-lung transplants, although these may require enhanced or mod- ified immunosuppression to prevent obliterative bronchi- olitis, a possible manifestation of chronic rejection.42 Early rejection after transplantation is the most important risk factor for the development of bronchiolitis obliterans syn- drome although pathogenesis is unclear.43 Lung infec- tion,42 or oxidative stress and lack of glutathione43 may be factors in the aggravation or onset of bronchiolitis obliter- ans syndrome. Donor-specific tolerance, whereby the patient permanent- ly accepts their graft without the need for long-term immu- nosuppression, while remaining immunocompetent, re- mains the ultimate goal in cardiac transplantation.6,9 1.
